4.3.2 Marginally Trapped LFS Population within a PENeLOPE Cycle

Marginally trapped low-field seeker neutrons (MT LFS), also known as MT UCNs through-
out this thesis, are UCNs that have total energies above the magneto-gravitational trapping
potential of 115 neV. It is of significant interest to track MT UCNs throughout an experiment
cycle because they are the focus of this precision study on the neutron lifetime measurement
using PENeLOPE. If they are lost during storage through wall interactions they cause a
systematic shift of the neutron lifetime measurement discussed in Section 4.2.5. The MT
LFS population is characterized by the ratio

RMT = MT LFS Population
Total LFS Population . (4.13)

Similarly to the p trend, RMT is plotted for the same run cycles used in the polarization
ratio analysis in section 4.3.1, as shown in Figures 4.27 and 4.28. The same marker col-
ors representing as in the polarization plots for each βSS are chosen for theses figures. In
a PENeLOPE experiment cycle, the LFS population is divided by a trapping potential
threshold into magnetically trapped and marginally trapped LFSs. The total trapping en-
ergy threshold of 80 neV, set by the absorber rings before the ramp-up stage, compensates
for the energy shift caused by the magnetic field, which is activated later in the ramp-up
stage. This shift increases the total energy of LFSs by approximately 35 neV, as shown
in Fig. 4.10. LFSs exceeding this energy threshold are classified as marginally trapped in
the experiment cycle when the magnetic field is turned off. When the magnetic field is ac-

101



tive, the trapping energy threshold rises to 115 neV, so LFSs above this new threshold are
considered marginally trapped.

1. Filling: Incoming MT LFSs from the spin flipper enter the storage volume at a higher
rate before the slower UCNs reach the storage volume, but this isn’t a significant effect
that would change RMT by much after a few seconds into the stage. The MT LFS
population decreases primarily due to the absorbers positioned at a height of 700 mm,
which remove MT LFSs (>80 neV), while also cleaning out some magnetically stored
LFSs above 70 neV for an added safety margin. MT LFSs are also considered lost if
they spin-flip into HFSs on wall reflections.

2. MT Cleaning: Since no additional UCNs are produced after the filling stage, a
decrease in RMT is apparent as the MT LFSs are cleaned by absorbers and lost through
wall reflections. The MT LFS population rapidly declines, with RMT values dropping
to below approximately 1 % in Fig. 4.28. Following this initial decrease, the loss
rate is smaller because the generation of MT LFSs from spin-flipped HFSs becomes
more pronounced in the reduced MT LFS population. By the end of the cleaning
stage, RMT decreases further to below 0.01%. The absorbers effectively eliminate MT
LFSs resulting in a storable LFS population exceeding 99.99 % after 199 s seconds
when considering only the number of LFS within the storage volume because RMT

ignores the number of HFSs. This statistical loss process can be modeled by one or
more exponential decay function(s) because the rate of absorption is proportional to
the number of neutrons leading to exponential behavior. The decreasing MT LFS
population trend is shown in Fig. 4.28 as an initially steep downward trend that
gradually flattens, the slope becoming less negative over time.

3. Ramp-up: The magnetic field increases during ramp-up causing LFSs to gain ∼35 neV.
This increase is due to the reduced phase space volume available to LFSs as the mag-
netic field strengthens, leading to a redistribution of their energy as discussed in
section 4.2.3. The MT cutoff is 80 neV before the linear ramping phase and 115 neV
afterwards. The MT cutoff is linearly interpolated between those values during ramp-
ing. The MT LFS fraction population increases with higher βSS. Spin flips reduce the
effectiveness of the MT cleaning phase, creating more MT LFS than can be cleaned.

4. HFS Cleaning: Cleaning HFSs reduces the likelihood of their spin-flipping into MT
LFSs. The decrease in the MT LFS population during this stage is primarily attributed
to wall reflections, while the absorbers, which move to the middle and bottom posi-
tions, also contribute to the cleaning of some MT LFSs. However, since the duration
of this stage is only 40 s for A and B combined, it does not significantly reduce the
MT fraction.

102



5. Storage: If MT LFSs are lost during this stage, they contribute to a systematic shift
of the measured τst so minimizing this population is crucial for a precise measurement
of τst. For βSS = 2×10−3, there are still more than 10 % marginally trapped neutrons
present at the start of the storage stage. The difference in RMT values between the
runs with different βSS values is seen more clearly in Fig. 4.28 on a log scale. RMT is
lower for lower values of βSS.

6. Ramp-down and Counting: Higher energy neutrons can reach the detectors earlier,
since they can overcome the magnetic barrier earlier during ramp-down. Therefore,
RMT drops inside the storage volume as well as in the cumulative detector counts.

The correlation between βSS and RMT is evident: a lower βSS value decreases the MT
LFS population within the storage volume. Consequently, a lower βSS is expected to reduce
the systematic shift of τst which is influenced by the loss of MT LFSs during the storage
stage.

The MT cleaning stage shows the expected exponential behavior for reducing the MT
LFS population. No significant difference is observed between the three curves for the three
different βSS values during the MT cleaning phase, likely because the spin-flip effect, which
would convert LFSs to HFSs or vice versa, is not as dominant as the absorber-induced loss
effect.

4.3.3 Optimizing the Marginally Trapped Cleaning Time

The neutron lifetime measurement is influenced by systematic effects due to loss processes,
other than β-decay, between 20 s and 1550 s during the storage stage. This has been dis-
cussed in detail in Section 4.2.5. Low-field seekers that are marginally trapped (MT LFSs)
and high-field seekers (HFSs) may be lost through wall interactions during the storage stage.
The magnetically stored LFSs that do not hit the walls are lost only through β−decay or
rest gas interaction. Rest gas interaction is not in the scope of this work and can be found
in [2].

The duration of each cleaning stage affects the number of MT LFSs and HFSs that
survive to the storage stage. This study focuses on optimizing the duration of the MT
cleaning stage to reduce the amount of MT LFSs lost during storage, thereby minimizing
the systematic shift of the measured neutron lifetime ∆τn. In this study, we focus on the
effect of marginally trapped LFSs only. Due to the much smaller number of UCN simulated
compared to a full run at FRM II, high statistical uncertainty was the leading reason to
filter out β−decay from storage stage simulation data for this study. Hence, loss mechanisms
due to MT LFSs have a contribution to the measured storage lifetime of

Minimizing the Systematic Effect Due to Marginally Trapped Neutrons

τMT is the average storage lifetime of all LFS in PENeLOPE during the storage period only
taking into account wall interactions of MT neutrons. Reducing the number of marginally
trapped LFSs in PENeLOPE during the storage stage lowers their impact on the neutron
lifetime measurement by decreasing losses, thereby increasing their storage lifetime τMT.
Consequently, the reduced loss of marginally trapped LFSs decreases this systematic effect,
effectively lowering its contribution to the shift in the measured neutron lifetime, ∆τn.

Each experiment cycle, with different stage times before the storage stage, has its own
τMT. The MT cleaning time is varied in this study, while all other times are taken from Tbl.
4.1. An optimization routine to find the minimum shift ∆τn becomes increasingly difficult as
more stage durations are varied and is out of the scope of this work. This will be investigated
in the future. The range of MT cleaning duration times examined is [0,199] s. During this
stage, the MT LFS population is removed from the storage volume at an exponential rate.

4.3.5 Simulation Conclusions

A PENeLOPE experiment as it could be conducted using the FRM II UCN source was sim-
ulated using PENTrack. The systematic shift of the neutron lifetime measurement produced
by the MT LFS population was reduced by optimizing the MT cleaning stage duration in
an experiment cycle. Three separate PENeLOPE simulations with different values of the
spin flip probability of stainless steel βSS were used as there is currently no measurement
available that has been verified.

Maximum τMT storage lifetimes representing the loss rate of the MT LFS population
during the storage stage determined for each βSS simulation were used to calculate the MT
LFS population’s contribution to the systematic shift.

The only observed systematic shift below the precision goal is seen when βSS = 10−5

with a shift value of ∆τn = 0.0442± 0.0019 s and with the cycle having a MT cleaning stage
duration of 113 s. Using these values, the optimal number of runs required to achieve the
statistical precision goal was determined to be 14. The spin flip probability of the storage
walls will have to be measured with PENeLOPE in situ and if found to be above 10−5, the
storage volume will have to be coated with e.g. NiP to reduce spin flips.

The method of varying only the MT cleaning stage duration is a limited one-parameter
optimization, as the other stage durations could potentially be varied. Optimizing over
multiple parameters could lead to an even smaller systematic effect on the neutron lifetime
measurement.

In this study's simulations the neutron counts in the filling, ramp-up, and storage stages
are lower than the actual UCN counts expected when filling PENeLOPE from the FRM II
source. The lifetime method of calculating UCN counts proved to be more valuable than
connecting the stages together through energy distribution plots as some UCN counts might
be missing due to insufficient statistics. It would be beneficial to study the loss mechanisms
using a simulation without spin-flip probabilities on any walls in the apparatus, allowing for

120



an assessment of the systematic shift on the neutron lifetime measurement unaffected by
spin flips. The results from this study would be compared with results from other simulations
with spin-flip probabilities included to see the impact of spin-flips on the systematic effects.

Simulation of the HFS cleaning stage is also limited by PENTrack’s inability to simulate
moving absorbers, leading to discontinuous changes in the UCN energy distributions. UCNs
reflecting from a moving absorber could shift their kinetic energies from the absorbers
momentum. Despite these caveats, important conclusions can be drawn from the simulations
already for reaching the precision goal with systematic effects and statistical reach.

121



Chapter 5

Conclusion and Outlook

PENeLOPE is a UCN bottle experiment, designed to measure the β-decay lifetime of free
neutrons τn with a precision target of 0.1 s. In 2022, three UCN transport components
(one UCN guide and two butterfly shutters, BS1 and BS2) were tested at TRIGA Mainz
to evaluate their suitability as PENeLOPE components. A storage lifetime experiment was
performed to characterize them. The experiment was conducted over two days, with Day 1
yielding τ = 11.52+0.42 /−0.43 s and Day 2 τ = 12.54+0.74 /−0.76 s. τst was significantly
lower than other guides characterized to be over 40 s [22].

The averaged relative leak rates of the butterfly shutters from two different experiments
were 2.23 ± 1.10 % and 1.01 ± 0.85 % for BS1 and BS2 respectively, making them unsuit-
able in their current state compared to other shutters, with relative leak rates below 10−3

[37]. Whether or not the replica guides are considered suitable cannot be judged from the
measured τst values, since leaks in the butterfly shutters alone do not account for the total
reduction in the lifetime. A follow up experiment conducted at ILL in 2023 with alternative
guides and shutters achieved improved storage lifetimes and leak rates [36].

PENeLOPE experiment cycles were simulated using PENTrack to analyze the system-
atic effects induced by marginally trapped low-field-seeking neutrons (MT LFSs). System-
atic shifts from three different simulation campaigns using different spin flip probabilities
on wall bounce βSS = {2 × 10−3, 10−4, 10−5} were compared. A study of the smallest
achievable systematic shift from MT LFSs on the measured storage lifetime τst was done
by adjusting the MT cleaning stage duration for each cycle. The precision goal of 0.1 s
was only achievable with a βSS = 10−5 simulation cycle resulting in a systematic shift of
∆τn = 0.0442 ± 0.0019 s. Higher values of βSS produced shifts exceeding the precision goal,
highlighting the need for further measurements of βSS if PENeLOPE’s surface material
stays the same. If the value of the spin-flip probability per wall bounce on stainless steel
of βSS = 3.36 · 10−3 from [24] is confirmed, the storage surfaces in PENeLOPE will require
coating to have a lower βSS value. A viable candidate for coating the storage surfaces would
be Nickel Phosphorous (NiP) which has been shown to have a spin flip probability as low
as βNiP on SS = 3.3+1.8

−5.6 · 10−6 [25].

122



Using the βSS = 10−5 configuration with the optimized systematic shift, the number
of experimental runs required to achieve a statistical precision of 0.1 s was determined.
A statistical uncertainty of σst = 0.0964 ± 0.0012 s is achieved in 14 runs assuming the
estimated UCN yield from the planned source at the FRM II in Garching, Germany.

These findings are currently limited by the simplified PENeLOPE model used in PEN-
Track simulations. Future simulations will incorporate the PENeLOPE CAD model devel-
oped for apparatus fabrication. Ongoing upgrades to PENTrack will also enable moving
geometries, allowing for more accurate modeling of absorber motion during the HFS clean-
ing stage. Improved analysis could be achieved by simulating a higher number of neutrons
in the storage stage. Planned future simulation studies include: 1. PENeLOPE simulations
will include a geometry of the TUCAN source at TRIUMF to assess the time required to
meet the precision goal using the anticipated TUCAN UCN source. 2. Future coil tests
on PENeLOPE at TRIUMF will provide new values of the magnetic field strength. For
this work, ideal magnetic field values were simulated so new simulations with corrected
magnetic field values will have to be done. 3. Studies of the experiment cycle with varying
durations of the two high-field-seeker cleaning stages (two absorber positions) are planned
to evaluate their contribution to the systematic shift on τst. 4. A comprehensive optimiza-
tion routine of varying all stage durations will be done to further reduce systematic effects
while maintaining low statistical uncertainty per cycle.

In mid-2024, the PENeLOPE experiment moved from TUM to TRIUMF for cryostat
testing, with a planned cooldown phase set for late 2025. The magnet must still be qualified
to sustain at least 50% of its nominal current. A separate coil testing experiment CoTEx
from previous PENeLOPE studies, demonstrated that achieving the nominal current may
not be possible in PENeLOPE’s setup [48]. The qualification of a nominal current of 50%
is a lower estimate of what is deemed realistic and worthy of continuing PENeLOPE’s
operation at TRIUMF. Initial UCN storage experiments are projected to begin by 2027,
after the long shutdown of the TRIUMF cyclotron in 2026.

abstracts.value: This paper presents the design, implementation, and experimental validation of a scalable 64-channel ultra-stable bipolar current supply for precision magnetic field control, developed for the TUCAN neutron electric dipole moment (nEDM) experiment. The system employs four 16-channel LTC2668 digital-to-analog converters and precision analog feedback circuitry to deliver independently programmable currents of up to ±40 mA per channel. The architecture emphasizes long-term stability, channel-to-channel consistency, and scalability for large coil arrays. Experimental validation includes long-term stability measurements and a scale-model coil experiment, demonstrating excellent agreement between measured and simulated magnetic fields. The measured current stability exceeds experimental requirements by more than an order of magnitude. The proposed system provides a robust instrumentation platform for high-channel-count precision magnetic field control and is applicable to a broad class of scientific and industrial systems requiring ultra-stable multi-channel current sources.

Executive summary

Antiprotonic helium. During 2025, 8 transitions in antiprotonic helium were studied or searched
for by laser spectroscopy. The laser systems were partially disassembled and reinstalled to conform
to updated CERN safety standards which took a lot of time and e!ort. Following the numerous up-
grades and modifications of our antiproton beamline, experimental target, and lasers, we measured
the laser resonances of antiprotonic helium with far higher signal-to-noise ratio, signal stability and
reproducibility, and data-taking speed compared to any previous experiment, even compared to
2024. This puts ASACUSA in concrete footing to an improved measurement of the antiproton-
to-electron mass ratio. ASACUSA installed several radiofrequency and atomic clocks which have
a frequency stability of order 10↑12. At the moment of antiproton production and injection into
AD, spurious shifts of at least 10↑11 were observed during the comparisons between the clocks.
We have apparently solved this issue but an optical reference signal provided from France and
Switzerland by optical fibre would eventually greatly benefit these e!orts as optical signals will be
more immune to this noise in the context of laser spectroscopy. Optical references also have the
short-term frequency stability needed to precisely measure the energies of these antiprotonic atoms
that have microsecond-scale lifetimes.
Antihydrogen.
Following the large increase of the antihydrogen beam intensity observed in 2024, the spectrometer
line consisting of a microwave cavity and a sextupole magnet was installed. Improvements of the
mixing process helped to partly compensate the intensity drop created by the factor 2 increased
distance between mixing region and antihydrogen detector, we typically observe 150 antihydrogen
atoms per 17 minute cycle. A preliminary analysis of the 2024 time-of-flight (ToF) data yielded
a broad velocity distribution with average velocities of about 2500m/s, significantly above the
limit of our spectrometer. As the analysis indicated a sizable fraction of ground-state atoms, a
first microwave on/o! experiment was attempted, but without success. Further ToF measurements
were performed and the focusing e!ect of the sextupole magnet was investigated. A new model-
independent cumulative analysis of the 2025 data was performed, confirming the high velocity of
the antihydrogen atoms. As a consequence for 2026 measures will be taken to improve the signal-
to-noise ratio, and to try to reduce the mean velocity of the antihydrogen atoms by optimizing the
mixing process.
Antiprotonic atom x-ray spectroscopy.
A new project is being developed to perform high-precision x-ray spectroscopy of transitions be-
tween Rydberg states in antiprotonic atoms to probe strong-field QED. The physics campaigns
will be conducted post LS3 at the ASACUSA-1 beamline, coupling a low-pressure gas cell with a
large area Transition Edge Sensor (TES) microcalorimeter detector. During the 2025-2026 period,
test beams are being conducted in the TELMAX zone with a simplified setup, protoype TES, and
multi-minibunch (MMBE) antiproton extraction. During the 2025 beamtime, antiprotonic atom
x-ray cascades were successfully observed with the TES for antiprotonic Zr and Si, validating the
experimental approach. Quantification of the beam-induced systematic e!ects is ongoing, as well
as finalization of the beamline design and integration of the experiment in the ASACUSA-1 zone
on a new parasitic beamline to be shared with the annihilation cross section measurements.
Annihilation cross sections.
The ASACUSA collaboration proposes a measurement of antiproton–nucleus annihilation cross
sections at the kinetic energy of 100 keV using micro-bunched beams from the ELENA decelerator.
This measurement addresses a region where experimental data are scarce and largely limited to
upper limits, while theoretical models remain poorly constrained. The approach builds on time-
resolved identification of in-flight annihilations, a technique successfully demonstrated in previous



ASACUSA campaigns, and benefits from the improved beam quality provided by ELENA.
The experiment will be installed in the ASACUSA-1 area on a parasitic beamline foreseen for

construction during LS3. Ultra-thin targets and an upgraded scintillator-based detector will enable
e”cient background suppression and precise normalization of the antiproton flux. The experimental
concept and apparatus layout have been defined, detector and target components are available or
under construction, and beamline integration studies are ongoing. In 2026, the collaboration plans
to start construction of the new scintillator detector, with first physics data expected once ELENA
operation becomes available after LS3.
Antiproton interferometry and the Aharonov-Bohm E!ect.
ASACUSA o!ers the possibility of studying antiprotons at low energy and in particular performing
quantum-interferometric studies and exploring the Aharonov-Bohm e!ect. In ASACUSA this can
be done by exploiting the slow (250 eV) antiproton beam that can be made available. At this energy,
quantum interference can be studied by means of material gratings and a high-resolution detector.
In addition, once the interferometric approach has been demonstrated, the addition of a magnetic
flux configuration (magnetized bars) will make possible the demonstration of the Aharonov-Bohm
e!ect for the antiproton.

This activity will involve the collaboration of two external group, which will join the ASACUSA
collaboration specifically to the purpose of realizing AIABE.

Antiprotonic Helium

1 Introduction

Antiprotonic helium is a three-body exotic atom that consists of a helium nucleus, an electron
occupying the 1s state, and an antiproton occupying a state with principal and orbital angular
momentum quantum numbers (n → ω+1 → 38) [1–12]. Studies of antihydrogen probe the interaction
between an antihadron and antilepton, whereas measurements of pHe+ is complementary, it being
a hadron-antihadron system having the longest known lifetime [13–19]. ASACUSA has
previously measured the transition frequencies of the atom εexp to a fractional precision of (2.3 ↑
16)↓ 10↑9, and by comparing the results with QED calculations, the antiproton-to-electron mass

In 2024 ASACUSA demonstrated synthesis of factor → 10 higher-density samples of pHe+ atoms

compared to the pre-ELENA era in a low-density helium gas target. Laser spectroscopy of the
transition (n, ω) = (35, 33)↔(34, 32) was carried out. Due to the high intensity and small emittance
of the ELENA beam, the event accumulation rate was> 10 times higher and the signal-to-noise ratio
far exceeded the typical values of past ASACUSA experiments using the radiofrequency decelerator
to slow down the antiprotons from 5.3 MeV to 100 keV [14]. A resonance profile that would have
taken → 2 weeks to accumulate at low densities of the gas target was measured in less than a day
of beamtime.

2 Laser spectroscopy measurements in 2025

In 2025 the collaboration further increased the production rate of pHe+ by factor 1.5↓ compared to
2024 by, a): installing Cherenkov and scintillation counters to detect the annihilation of antiprotons
along the electrostatic transport beamline, and use the information to e”ciently steer the beam
to the target. Unwanted antiproton annihilations in the di!erential pumping irises and electrodes
were thus minimized, b): installing magnetic shielding along the 12 m long beamline to reduce the
e!ects of stray magnetic fields of typically B = 1.0↑ 1.5 gauss that were influencing the antiproton
beam and causing systematic changes in the experimental signal over time (or when the overhead
crane ran over our experiment). Several improvements were made to the cryogenic helium target.

Following the rearrangement and recommissioning of the lasers in our laser hut required by
CERN safety, laser spectroscopy of the transition (n, ω) = (35, 33)↔(34, 32) was again demonstrated
(see Fig. 2). Due to numerous improvements in the antiproton beamline and the lasers, a far better
resonance signal was rapidly measured compared to 2024. The data acquisition rate, spectral
resolution, reproducibility, and signal-to-noise ratio of the observed spectra are superior to any
previous experiment on antiprotonic helium using low-density helium gas targets. The results
including the new experimental data firmly put ASACUSA on the path towards improvement of
the antiproton-to-electron mass ratio. The experiments were repeated with two Ti:Sapphire laser
systems, one of which was newly constructed in 2025.

Fig. 3 shows the measured intensity of the laser resonance signal as a function of the density of

the target, and minimize the number of antiprotons that stop in the entrance window [20] and cause
background annihilations. Theoretical groups of Helsink University are currently collaborating with
us to model the passage of antiprotons through the entrance window and optimize the foil material
and thickness.

3.2 Optical and radiofrequency metrology

In 2025, ASACUSA installed two ultrastable, ultra-low noise quartz oscillators and two economical
rubidium atomic radiofrequency clocks in the laser hut that are referenced to GPS satellites. This
calibration system is necessary to measure the optical frequencies of our lasers that interrogate the
atom. Comparison measurements between the four clocks found that though a long-term stability of
→ 10↑12 was achieved (not yet verified in terms of absolute accuracy) when the clocks were allowed
to run over several days, once every 100 seconds a spurious deviation of order 10↑11 was detected
(see Fig. 5). This sudden deviation occurred in synchronization with antiproton production and
injection into AD, and did not occur at other times. We therefore magnetically shielded our atomic
clocks, cables, and counters, and optimized the time constants of the phase-lock loop servos in the
clocks. This reduced the unwanted noise below the detection limit, but indicates that proper care
is needed to carry out ultraprecise measurements in the environment of the AD.

3.3 Beamline

We are working with Paris researchers to implement the PAX experiment of x-ray spectroscopy of
antiprotonic atoms in a parasitic beamline branch of the antiprotonic helium experiment. For this
an electrostatic bending element is being designed, and a quadrupole triplet is under construction
in London. The beamline will also house the antiproton annihilation experiment described later in
the report.

The collaboration continued construction of the induction decelerator to slow down the antipro-
tons. When this is installed, the background annihilations that occur in the walls of the experi-
mental apparatus may be carefully reduced so that the signal-to-noise ratio of the laser resonance
signal may be improved by another factor 2–3.

2 Antiprotons

2.1 Antiproton Trapping in MUSASHI and Transport to the Cusp Trap

The AD/ELENA delivered 13 ↓ 106 p per cycle for most of the 2025 beam time. The number of
cooled p in the MUSASHI trap was > 3↓ 106 per one AD/ELENA spill. The p catching e”ciency
of MUSASHI was often degraded due to perturbations in the ambient magnetic field of the AD

8



hall causing a misalignment of the beam into MUSASHI necessitating frequent re-steering. These
perturbations were from magnetic field changes from other collaborations, the overhead crane, etc.,
as discussed in Sec. 2.3.

In order to synthesize H atoms, the best scheme for p in ASACUSA is stacking several ELENA
shots in MUSASHI and then transferring to the Cusp trap. Manipulations in the Penning-Malmberg
trap potentials and rotating walls (RW) were tuned to suppress losses during stacking. Stacking
four ELENA shots reached 12↓ 106 p in MUSASHI in 2025.

In addition, a multiple-extraction scheme has been developed to improve the e”ciency of p
transfer between the MUSASHI and Cusp traps. Although there were still losses during the op-
eration, the best approach was to split the plasma in two, compress radially, and extract the
downstream-most p plasma to the Cusp trap after e↑ removal. By repeating this cycle three times,
more than 7↓ 106 p were routinely prepared in the Cusp trap for the H experiment.

2.2 Scintillating Bar Detectors

The scintillating bar detector is used to monitor the time and vertex position of antiproton anni-
hilations in the Cusp trap by detecting the charged pions produced in the process. It consists of
8 planes of extruded scintillating bars with active areas between 0.5 and 1 m2, arranged around
the Cusp trap in four “X–Y” modules to allow three-dimensional reconstruction of pion tracks.
Scintillation light is collected via WLS fibers and read out by SiPMs, providing a vertex position
resolution of approximately 5 cm [23]. During 2025, the detector was operated throughout the
beam time and used for routine monitoring of trapping and annihilation processes. A dedicated
calibration run (see Fig. 8) was performed to validate the reliability of the reconstructed annihi-
lation position. For the 2026 data-taking period, only limited software developments are foreseen,

mainly aimed at improving integration with other experimental subsystems and increasing the level

Building on the experience accumulated during long term operation in antihydrogen formation
experiments, the new system will feature higher overall e”ciency thanks to the use of cast plastic

and new front-end electronics. Some dedicated modules will be installed along the antihydrogen

2.3 Magnetic Field Logging

An array of magnetometers has been installed during the 2025 run to monitor variations of the mag-
netic field in the ASACUSA experimental zone due to AD and ELENA operation, crane movements,
and configuration changes of the other experiments in the hall. This information is particularly
important for p beam steering and catching in the MUSASHI trap. The magnetic-field data was
regularly referenced during the run to optimize the p catching e”ciency under each condition.

The system consists of six magnetometers, either fluxgate sensors or Hall sensors enhanced by
integrated magnetic concentrators (IMC) (Triaxis↭). The less expensive Hall-IMC sensor (250 nT
resolution) was found to be su”ciently sensitive to study the magnetic-field variations of interest.
The acquired data is stored in a PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB database optimized for time-series data.

3 Positron Beamline

The positron system underwent several minor changes within 2025, resulting in a small improvement
in performance. This is important for replenishing the positron reservoir used in the H mixing cycle
before antiproton stacking is finished, as shown in Fig. 13. A detailed outline of the system can
be found in Refs. [25] and [22] and a schematic overview is shown in Fig. 7. As a reminder, a
22Na source is moderated with solid Ne to create a slow e+ beam; the DC beam is pulsed using
a Surko-type bu!er gas trap (BGT) which is filled with positrons for 1 s; around one-hundred
positron bunches from the BGT are transferred into and stored in a Penning-Malmberg trap called
the accumulator, before being sent to the Cusp trap. The significant changes made to the positron
beam in 2025 are given in the following list:

• To try and reduce the decay rate of the Ne moderator, which was >5% per day in 2024, two
changes were made to the beamline. Firstly, the di!erential pumping between the BGT and
Ne moderator was improved to limit the amount of trap gas reaching the source. Additionally,
the automated Ne flow regulator was replaced with a manual needle valve, as the automatic
system was identified as a potential source of contamination in the system. The moderator
decay rate did not improve after these changes, and the cause of this issue remains unidentified.

• The number of positrons accumulated in the BGT was improved by 25% by adding an addi-
tional electromagnetic coil to better steer the DC positrons into the electrode stack.

• The positron cloud in the BGT expanded when it was moved from an initial electrostatic well
at the position of the rotating wall (RW) in which DC positrons were collected, downstream to
a second well used to dump the positrons to the accumulator. The movement of the positrons
during the dumping procedure was minimised by keeping them in the same spatial location
with the same well shape so the RW would continue providing compression. The number of
positrons transferred from the BGT to the positron accumulator was improved by 13% due
to this change.

12



• The positron accumulator can now hold twice as many positrons as last year, more than 21
million, due to the use of a deeper electrostatic well. The 398 ± 7 s lifetime in this well is
still su”cient to stack positrons for the 100s long H production.

The channeltron previously used to measure the e”ciency of the neon moderator, was found
to be under-counting positrons. This led to an underestimation of the moderator e”ciency and
an overestimation of the BGT e”ciency last year [22]. Therefore, quantifying the e”ciency of the
system for every stage is not possible, and hence the e”ciency of positron stacking in the Cusp trap
relative to the source strength will be given. The source strength was 1.13 GBq as of December
2025, and we stacked 21 million positrons in the Cusp trap for a total accumulation time of 100 s
in the BGT. That equates to an e”ciency of ↗ 0.02% when taking into account the 90% branching
ratio of ϖ+ decay from the 22Na source. The maximum e”ciency of the system based on the
quoted e”ciencies of the First Point Scientific Inc. Ne moderator and BGT, and our own measured
e”ciency of the positron accumulator of ↗95% would be 0.05%. So there is at least a factor of two
e”ciency increase to be found in our system. However, at the end of 2024 it took 10.3 minutes to
stack 100 million positrons, compared to 11.5 minutes in 2025, i.e. a small increase in duration
compared to the 23% decrease in source strength over that time period, so some improvement has
been made.

During the 2026 beam time the emphasis will be on H physics. The positron beam will therefore
be recommissioned in February, once cooling water is returned to the AD, and used for H production
until the end of Run 3. Providing as many positrons as possible, as reliably as possible, will
continue to be important for the H program during LS3 and beyond. During LS3 improvements for
the beamline are planned in order to minimise the e!ect of a continuously decaying source. This
includes: (i) improving the BGT lifetime which is currently only 1.52 ± 0.07 s, (ii) identifying and
resolving the cause of the rapid moderator decay, (iii) integrating feedback from the new ambient
magnetic field monitoring system to minimise the losses caused by the overhead crane (Sec. 2.3),
and more.

4 Cusp trap & H production

Using the slow-merge mixing method [26] the 2025 standard mixing cycle, shown in Fig. 13, merged
more than 7↓106 p with around 1.3↓108 e+. This cycle produced approximately 4↓106 H within
the Cusp trap over the mixing period of 120 s. This is a factor of 2.5 increase in p and almost a
factor of 2 increase in the total H-yield, for which changes to the hardware and techniques used in
the Cusp trap were necessary.

Fig. 13 shows a timeline of the processes involved in one mixing cycle. First the Cusp was
filled, or replenished, with e+. Meanwhile four bunches of p were caught in the MUSASHI trap and
prepared for transfer to the Cusp trap. When the e+ loading was completed, the p were transferred
and stored upstream (towards MUSASHI and away from the spectroscopy beamline) of the e+ in
the Cusp. Rotating wall compression, cyclotron cooling of positrons, sympathetic cooling of p, as
well as purification of both species (e↑ removal from p and ion removal from e+) was performed
after loading to prepare the plasmas for H production. The cold, compressed and purified p and
e+ plasmas were slowly merged together in a 120 s mixing cycle in two stages, see below. Unused
p that accumulated upstream and downstream of the e+ well were pushed to the first field null
of the double Cusp trap where the magnetic field is almost zero and confinement is lost resulting
in annihilation where counting could be performed to measure the H production e”ciency. The
remaining e+ were replenished for subsequent runs as most are not used up during mixing.

4.1 e+ purification

Positive ions are present within the positron plasma which causes the positron temperature to be
high leading to less e”cient H production, necessitating their removal. The purification technique
involves placing the positrons into an initial well with a potential barrier between it and a second,
final well, see Fig. 14. By repeatedly lowering and raising the barrier between the initial and final
e+ wells by applying a short voltage pulse on the time scale of 100 ns the light and fast e+ were
gradually transferred to the final well, leaving behind the heavy and slow ions. The well depths
were adjusted throughout the process to compensate for the change in the local space charge of the
plasmas.

During the 2024 beam time the number of p that could be used for mixing in the Cusp trap was
limited by this e+ purification technique. For the potential well configuration of the trap needed
to separate the e+ from the ions at electrode u10, the p had to be moved into u13, see Fig. 14(c),
which bordered the meshes shielding our trap from microwaves which can heat the plasmas. The
contact with these meshes led to a high annihilation rate and losses of p during e+ purification.
Multiple plasma manipulations were necessary to e!ectively remove ions and to minimize the loss
of antiprotons. These additional movements introduced additional complexity and increased the
duration of the mixing cycle by more than a minute [22].

In 2025 the ion removal routine was moved to a di!erent section of the trap, enabling more
p to be used. The barrier electrode was shifted from electrode u10 to u5, see Fig. 14(b). As a
result, the direction in which the e+ were extracted, was reversed. This change led to a much more
compact well configuration. The revised method also reduced the amplitude, and increased the
number of times the voltage pulse could be applied to the barrier, reducing the heating of the e+

during the process and consequently the time required to purify the plasma as it was no longer
necessary to wait for the positrons to cool between each voltage pulse which could take 8 s. The
final temperature of the e+ plasma was the same using this revised scheme as it was in the 2024
beam time.

5.1 Microwave Cavity

A distinct feature of ASACUSA is to conduct the antihydrogen hyperfine spectroscopy in a beam.
Therefore, the interaction region must be separated from the strong electric and magnetic fields of
the mixing trap. This is a key advantage, as the homogeneity of the static magnetic field in the
interaction region is crucial for the achievable experimental precision. The interaction volume is a
cylinder of 100mm in diameter and 105.5mm long (which corresponds to half the wavelength of
the 1.42GHz ground state hyperfine transition in hydrogen). It is situated inside a strip-line cavity,
where the oscillating magnetic field Bosc is produced transversally to the beam axis. Around the
cavity, a set of McKeehan coils produces the static magnetic field Bstat used for the precise control
of the Zeeman shift. Bstat is horizontal and orthogonal to the beam axis. Despite the advantage of
distancing the interaction region from the mixing trap, the spectroscopy apparatus must be kept
close to ensure a large detection solid angle. The microwave cavity and surrounding McKeehan coils
are encased in three layers of cylindrical mu-metal shielding. An additional set of coils is attached
between the outermost and middle layer of the mu-metal shielding on the up- and downstream
sides of the cavity. They create magnetic fields to compensate stray fields entering the interaction
region axially, thus increasing the homogeneity of the static magnetic background field (Fig. 16).

5.2 Magnetic Field Compensation

Measurements of the magnetic field inside the interaction region were conducted, yielding an average
total magnetic field strength of |Bstat| = 45.96(12) µT throughout the measured volume. The two
transitions ASACUSA aims to measure are the ϱ and ς transition of ground-state H (see Fig. 17).
The measured homogeneity of |Bstat| corresponds to a potential frequency shift of the ϱ resonance
of up to 0.586(6) kHz depending on the trajectories of the atoms through the interaction volume.
This is smaller than the initially aimed accuracy of 1 ppm.

5.3 Sextupole Magnet

A sextupole magnet [27] was installed on the downstream side of the microwave cavity for spin
selection before annihilation events are counted by the H beam detector. The conditioning of the
magnet was started in May 2025 and completed by September 2025.

5.4 Antihydrogen Beam Detector

The H detector consists of a BGO scintillator as central calorimeter, two plastic scintillator ho-
doscope layers along the beam axis, and orthogonal plastic scintillator tiles [22]. Pions from p
annihilation produce signals in the scintillators which are read out by SiPMs. For the BGO the
SiPMs are arranged across the disk. Hodoscope bars (EJ-200) have double-sided readouts in coin-
cidence to minimize noise, and hodoscope tiles (EJ-200) have single-sided readouts. This results in
a total of 432 TDC (time-to-digital converter) channels.

In 2025 the data acquisition (DAQ) system of the H detector underwent several upgrades. The
complete DAQ code was rewritten and simplified into a single C++ project that is controlled by
a python graphical user interface (GUI). The code combines the data from several CAEN V1190
TDCs and CAEN V2495 FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays) via a CAEN V4718 VME bridge
into a structured binary file. Additionally to the DAQ, the code for the initial analysis of the binary
data was redone. A second C++ project handles reading the data and converting it to a ROOT
file. Here the biggest upgrade was a change to a newer version of ROOT, allowing us to use the
modern RDataFrame interface for a quicker and simpler analysis. After each antihydrogen mixing
cycle, the analysis automatically creates plots showing the 2-dimensional distribution of hits on the
BGO, as well as counts over time displayed in the GUI.

The DAQ trigger requires at least one signal in the BGO, the inner and the outer bars. Therefore
both cosmics and annihilations upstream of the BGO can produce a trigger. Preliminary o#ine
analysis has revealed, that the signal to noise ratio can be increased by applying cuts on the BGO
data.

6 Antihydrogen Results

With the increased distance between production region and antihydrogen detector, we observe
about 150 antihydrogen candidates per mixing cycle of 17 minutes length. The data presented are
counts of the hardware trigger without further analysis.

6.1 Sextupole Focusing

Measurements were conducted to verify the focusing power of the sextupole magnet. Figure 18
shows the mean position of hits on the bismuth germanate oxide (BGO) scintillator for three
di!erent sextupole currents. The annihilation points are encircled by a white ring which shows
the width of a 2D Gaussian function fitted to the data. The e!ect of focusing by the sextupole is
clearly visible but small, indicating a high velocity of the H atoms.

6.2 Spectroscopy: Microwave On/O! Measurement

First estimates on the average H velocity were obtained in 2024 (preliminary results are described
in [28], details on the mixing process used are under review at Physics of Plasmas [29]). The
principles of this time of flight measurement are described below in sec. 6.3. For atoms in the
n ↫ 27 quantum states an average velocity of ↘v≃ = 2770(160)m/s was obtained, while atoms in
the 27 < n < 36 quantum state range led to an average velocity of ↘v≃ = 2440(150)m/s [28]. A
model-independent analysis of the 2025 data presented in sec. 6.3 yields similar velocities.

However, the relevant question is what this says about the velocity of ground-state H, which
are relevant for spectroscopy. Both the polarizing power of the Cusp field gradients [30–32] and
the analyzing power of the sextupole’s magnetic field gradients critically depend on the beam

By comparing the two velocities measured for di!erent quantum state ranges in 2024 [28], it was
assumed that lower principal quantum states are correlated to lower average velocities. Additionally,

Assuming further improvements of the beam intensity, an optimistic estimation for the number of

The sextupole magnet was powered with 350A and an estimated microwave power and frequency
corresponding to atoms with a velocity of 2000m/s and static magnetic fields of 0.46 µT was applied.
A successful microwave interaction turns low field seeking H into high field seeking ones to be
defocused by the sextupole magnet, thus leading to a drop in count rate on the H beam detector.

A signal generator was used in amplitude modulation mode switching between two set pow-
ers every second for two second periods. At the achieved statistics of around 4000 H atoms for
each microwave setting, no statistically significant drop in count rate with microwaves ‘on’ com-
pared to ‘o!’ could be observed. Figure 19 visualizes this result. An asymmetry parameter
(NOFF↑NON)/(NOFF+NON) was cumulatively summed and plotted against an increasing number
of measurements NON describes the number of atoms counted on the detector during a cycle where
microwaves were applied (on), while NOFF corresponds to the number of atoms counted during
a cycle without microwave interaction (o!). The asymmetry parameter can take values between
minus one and one. Successful microwave interactions raise the parameter above zero. At this level
of statistics a drop in count rate by ↗7% (i.e. NON ↗ 0.93NOFF) should have been detectable
with a 3 ϱ significance. Due to several background contributions it is plausible that the count rate
drop might be that small, especially if the velocity of ground-state H is 2000m/s or higher or the
ground-state fraction is smaller than estimated.

Part III

Antiprotonic atom x-ray spectroscopy

1 Introduction

Quantum electrodynamics (QED) is the foundational quantum field theory of the Standard Model.
It describes the interaction between charged particles and the quantum vacuum via two fundamental
processes: a) the self-energy (SE), wherein the charged particle emits and reabsorbs a virtual
photon, and b) the vacuum polarization (VP), wherein virtual leptonic particle-antiparticle pairs
are created in the Coulomb field of the nucleus. Both these interactions with the quantum vacuum
slightly modify atomic orbitals, and since the experiments of Lamb and Rutherford [34], we know
that one must account for these interactions to correctly describe the bound states of atoms.

While the exceptional agreement between QED theory and experiment has been obtained for
hydrogen and deuterium, allowing to test calculations of up to third order QED [35], when moving
to higher-Z systems for bound-state QED (BSQED) tests via spectroscopy of highly-charged ions
(HCIs), the theory is barely tested beyond first-order e!ects. Though, in principle, high-Z systems
should act as a magnifying glass for QED, as the QED contributions grow as Z4, numerous exper-
imental and theoretical problems currently prevent the full exploitation of this scaling law. On the
experimental side, the transition energies of HCI can be of the order of keV, and thus are outside of
the reach of laser spectroscopy. Furthermore, HCIs must be created at accelerator facilities, which
induces large Doppler shifts in the measured transition energies.

The theoretical methods used to describe these systems also face substantial challenges. Because
the interaction with the Coulomb field can no longer be treated in perturbation theory in the high-Z
regime, the QED e!ects must be calculated to all orders in the Coulomb interaction. Furthermore,
in HCIs, the levels with the largest QED shifts are closest to the nucleus, with considerable overlap
between the electron and nuclear wavefunctions. Since the nuclear properties of high-Z systems are
poorly known, the theoretical uncertainties in the transition energies coming from poorly known
nuclear charge radii and nuclear polarization can completely obfuscate second-order QED e!ects.
Together, these challenges have left the higher-order contributions in bound state strong-field QED
largely untested, which represents an open fundamental physics frontier and an impediment to the
numerous searches for new physics based on spectroscopy of heavy atoms and ions.

This project, called PAX (antiProtonic Atom X-ray spectroscopy), proposes a new paradigm for
testing strong-field BSQED by using the spectroscopy of antiprotonic atoms where the larger mass
of the antiproton produces a proportionally smaller Bohr radius in all states (mp̄

We aim thus to perform high-precision x-ray spectroscopy of the transitions between Rydberg
states in antiprotonic atoms to probe strong-field QED. The key technology for this experimental
program is a Transition Edge Sensor (TES) x-ray microcalorimeter array developed and fabricated
by the NIST Quantum Sensing Division (Boulder, Colorado, USA). TES microcalorimeters measure
the energy of individual photons through the temperature change of a superconducting thin film
thermometer, as shown in Figure 24. The TES thermometer is coupled to a photon absorber
composed of a high-Z element such as bismuth or tin, enabling high quantum e”ciency for x rays
up to and beyond 100 keV. The fundamental energy resolution of a calorimeter is proportional to√
kBT 2C, where T and C are the sensor temperature and heat capacity, respectively, allowing these

devices to achieve extraordinary energy resolution by operating at cryogenic temperatures [39].

2.1 Measurement of antiprotonic atom x rays

An initial two-week-long measuring campaign was conducted in May 2025. As a first test, the

Part IV

Annihilation cross sections of 100 keV
antiprotons

1 Introduction and Scientific Motivation

The ASACUSA collaboration proposes a new measurement of antiproton–nucleus annihilation cross
sections (ϱann) at the kinetic energy of 100 keV, making use of the ELENA decelerator in micro-
bunch mode, as described in Ref. [45]. This program continues a long-standing research line that
includes earlier measurements performed in ASACUSA at 5.3 MeV [46,47] and 125 keV [48,49].

The new experiment aims at providing absolute measurements of the antiproton annihilation
cross section at very low energies, where the existing dataset is largely limited to upper bounds
and remains insu”cient for current theoretical requirements.

The study of low–energy antiproton interactions is important for understanding the dynamics
of antimatter in the nuclear environment and for addressing questions that impact nuclear physics,
neutron–antineutron oscillation searches, and the interpretation of cosmic-ray antiprotons.

Since the existing dataset below the MeV scale remains limited, measurements at 100 keV o!er
an opportunity to expand experimental knowledge in a region where theoretical models are poorly
constrained. A detailed discussion of these motivations is presented in the document “ASACUSA
Proposal for Run4 and beyond” [45].

2 Experimental Method and Apparatus

2.1 Context and Measurement Strategy

Previous ASACUSA measurements have demonstrated the capability of time–based techniques
for identifying in-flight antiproton annihilations, enabling the measurement of annihilation cross
sections. At 5.3 MeV, the collaboration obtained the first pulsed–beam low–energy annihilation
data on several targets [46, 47], while the 125 keV campaign produced only upper limits due to
contamination of the bare–carbon target, an issue that prevented the extraction of absolute cross–
section values [49]. The ASACUSA results are shown in Figure 33 together with the other available
data at low and intermediate energies.

The limitations of the 125 keV campaign were due to experimental constraints rather than to
the time-of-flight method itself, and can be avoided in a new measurement at ELENA [45].

ELENA delivers 100 keV antiprotons in micro-bunches with su”ciently low intensity to allow
individual annihilation events in the thin target to be counted without saturating the detector. The
bunch timing also provides a clear temporal separation between the target signal and background
annihilations on the vacuum-chamber walls or at the beam dump (typically more than 140 ns and
about 390 ns later, respectively), see Figure 34.

The annihilation cross section will be determined from the number of in-flight annihilation
events occurring within the expected time window, together with precise measurements of the
number of incident antiprotons and of the target’s areal density.

2.3 Expected Performance

Given the expected rate of approximately one in-flight annihilation per 105 incident antiprotons

3 Plans for 2026

During 2025, the ASACUSA collaboration has consolidated the experimental concept for the mea-
surement of antiproton–nucleus annihilation cross sections at 100 keV using ELENA micro-bunched
beams. The measurement strategy, based on time separation of in-flight annihilations from back-
ground events, builds directly on techniques successfully demonstrated in previous ASACUSA cam-
paigns.

The apparatus layout in the ASACUSA-1 area has been defined; beamline integration is in
progress, and the design of a new high-performance scintillator-bar detector is ongoing. Key com-
ponents of the detection and target systems are already available or under construction.

In 2026, the collaboration plans to start the construction of the new scintillator detector and
the design of the parasitic beamline. First physics data at 100 keV are expected after LS3.

It should be noted that, beyond the measurement program described here, a complementary

1 Antiproton Interferometry and Aharonov-Bohm E!ect (AIABE)

ASACUSA o!ers a very interesting possibility, based on the 250 eV antiproton beam obtainable with
the MUSASHI trap, to be directed (with an Einzel lens system) to the positron transfer line. This
section provides a very low energy beam that can be used to perform interferometric experiments
with antiprotons. This proposal concerns the two steps of performing antiproton interferometry
first, followed by the study of the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) e!ect for antiprotons.

The first part will be realized by subjecting the 250 eV beam to the action of an interferometer
with a 1000 slits grating having an opening of 100 nm fo any slit and an interslit distance of 10 µm.
The di!racted particles will propagate in the 1 m long interferometer equipped with an emulsion
detector at the opposite end.

The interference pattern will be produced by reconstructing the ”vertex” trajectories of pions
generated by antiprotons hitting the emulsions. The grating system and the emulsion detectors
will be provided by groups external to ASACUSA and interested in AIABE.

The second part of the program is the demonstration of the magnetic AB e!ect for antiprotons.
The schematic concept of this experiment is shown in fig. 36. The magnetic flux required for the
detection of the e!ect will be provided by a magnetized bar.

Figure 36 – An example of the geometry for an experiment aimed to verify the magnetic AB e!ect.
With respect to the no-flux case (C), the presence of the magnetic potential induces a phase shift (C↑).

We are currently in the preparation phase, realizing a double/section experimental chamber to
be adapted to the ASACUSA beamline. This is necessary in order to comply with the vacuum
requirements of the experiment. The same chamber setup can be used for preparatory tests in
TELMAX, which is planned and will be useful in the first phase of the experiment.

During data taking, AIABE is not compatible with the normal ASACUSA functioning. How-
ever, the beam time requirement of interferometric experiments will only be of the order of a day.

abstracts.value:
This year, the Nobel Prize in Physics recognises the discovery of a diffuse flux of astrophysical
neutrinos, which extends to petaelectronvolt (PeV, $10^{15}$ eV) energies. Such neutrinos probe
cosmic-ray acceleration sites, where it is thought that highly relativistic protons or nuclei collide
with ambient matter or radiation to produce charged pions, which subsequently decay, producing
neutrinos. This milestone discovery in astroparticle physics has been made possible using data
recorded by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic-kilometre–sized detector located at a
depth of ~2 km in the polar ice, close to the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. IceCube is a
National Science Foundation (NSF)–managed research facility, operated as an international
collaboration involving ~450 people from 58 institutions in 14 countries.
Francis Halzen has long been the driving force behind the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. As
Principal Investigator from its beginnings, he has spearheaded the collective work by scientists
and engineers that resulted in a volume of instrumented Antarctic ice sufficiently large to detect
high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. His scientific vision thus provides the basis for new
research in the future of this field.

titles.title: Scientific Background to the Nobel Prize in Physics 2026: For Decisive Contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the Discovery of High-Energy Neutrinos of Astrophysical Origin

abstracts.value: Preparing quantum states from classical data can cost more than the computation they serve; most loaders tailor a circuit to each input. Here we show that the signals of a real dataset share structure that can be learned once and reused. Our quantum-native loader learns a low-dimensional description of a dataset and prepares every signal with one fixed circuit set by a few numbers. Across seven views of five public datasets it meets the targets of the strongest structured loader at equal gate cost with several times fewer numbers per signal. These numbers can be inferred from a random subset: in a preregistered blind replication the subset needed to come within ten per cent of full-signal accuracy stayed constant within a prespecified margin as signals grew sixteenfold, whereas the structured loader needed ever more. It declines what it cannot represent, covering fewer cases than that baseline and no electrocardiogram.

titles.title: Quantum data loading from the learned shared structure of real signals

abstracts.value: We study cyclic triorthogonal codes in prime dimension $p$, on which a transversal third-level diagonal gate acts as a logical non-Clifford gate. For odd $p$, we use a definition of triorthogonality that does not require self-orthogonality. For cyclic codes of length coprime to $p$, triorthogonality reduces to a sumset condition on the spectral support, which makes exhaustive search feasible: for two natural constructions, we enumerate all maximal codes of this kind for $p=3$ up to length $121$ and $p=5,7$ up to length $96$. For qubits, we prove that a cyclic code of odd length is triply even if and only if it is classically triorthogonal, giving a complete description of triply-even cyclic codes, and we determine all such codes up to length $763$. For qudits, we find codes such as $[[19,1,3]]_3$ and $[[7,1,3]]_7$, which improve on the shortest Reed-Muller and Reed-Solomon codes in both overhead exponent and distillation threshold. The latter is the first member of an infinite family of $[[p,1,2\lfloor p/6\rfloor+1]]_p$ codes.

titles.title: Cyclic triorthogonal codes in prime dimension

abstracts.value: Quantum query complexity enjoys a variety of pleasing joint computation properties: for example, a composition theorem asserting $Q(f\circ g)=Θ(Q(f)Q(g))$ for all Boolean functions $f$ and $g$; a direct sum theorem asserting that computing $k$ copies of a function (or search problem) costs $Ω(k)$ times as much as the cost of computing one copy; and a direct product theorem asserting that for Boolean functions, even succeeding at the direct sum problem with exponentially small probability still requires $Ω(k)$ times the cost of computing one copy to bounded error. However, all of these results are strictly for worst-case quantum query complexity. For example, if we have a fixed distribution $μ$ over inputs, the direct sum theorem says nothing about the quantum query complexity of computing $k$ copies of $f$ when the input comes from the product distribution $μ^k$ instead of being worst-case. (Note that while a standard Yao-type minimax theorem guarantees a hard distribution for the direct sum problem, there's no guarantee that this hard distribution is a product distribution.) A similar problem occurs for the direct product theorem and the composition theorem: none of these results respect distributions. In this work, we give distributional joint computation lower bounds for the composition, direct sum, and direct product problems. Along the way, we introduce some new tools for handling quantum query lower bounds, including (a) a new ``multiplicative'' variant of the $γ_2$ norm (which we use in place of the multiplicative adversary method for proving the direct product theorem), and (b) a new ``Shaltiel-free'' measure of quantum query complexity, which we show characterizes the composition behavior of distributional quantum query complexity and satisfies pleasing properties.

titles.title: Distributional Quantum Query Complexity

abstracts.value: Multimodal vision-language systems typically fuse image and text embeddings through classical operators such as concatenation, attention, bilinear pooling, or tensor interactions. We propose Quantum Entangled Multimodal Fusion Networks (QEMFN), a hybrid quantum-classical framework that introduces parameterized entanglement as a structured inductive bias for multimodal fusion. Pretrained visual and textual features are projected into compact latent spaces, encoded as angle-parameterized quantum states, processed through intra-modal and paired cross-modal entangling circuits, and measured to produce fused representations for retrieval. Under matched parameter budgets and identical frozen CLIP backbones, QEMFN outperforms classical fusion baselines on COCO-5k and Flickr30k, including multilayer perceptron, tensor fusion, FiLM, cross-attention, compact transformer, and a dequantized paired-topology analogue. An ablation suite isolates the quantum module's contribution from the surrounding classical projections, and quantum-centric analyses report Meyer-Wallach entangling capability, expressibility, gradient variance against barren-plateau bounds, and entropy-performance correlation under controls for training progress alongside an intervention study on the entangling component. QEMFN is executed under shot-based estimation, a noise-modeled fake backend, and a real superconducting device with zero-noise extrapolation. This work does not claim quantum computational advantage; the contribution is the framework together with a controlled empirical and quantum-centric evaluation that positions trainable entanglement as an interpretable, hardware-executable fusion mechanism at scales accessible on contemporary devices.

titles.title: Quantum Entangled Multimodal Fusion Networks (QEMFN): Resource-Aware Hybrid Vision-Language Fusion via Trainable Entanglement

abstracts.value: Superconducting circuits have emerged as one of the most promising and scalable platforms for quantum com- puting, with substantial industrial adoption driving qubit counts steadily upward. Yet the layout of the corresponding chips is still primarily performed manually, consuming multiple days or weeks of expert effort, even for moderately sized designs. Existing automation approaches sidestep this bottleneck by simplifying the underlying problem and relaxing physical constraints. Therefore, they fall short of fabrication-ready results. To overcome this scalability wall without such compromises, we first introduce a formal abstraction that translates physical device characteristics into a rigorous geometric problem formulation. This abstraction bridges physical realization and design automation. Building upon this abstraction, we then propose a three-stage design automation flow comprising geometry-aware global partitioning, ILP-based port assignment, and a hierarchical routing pipeline. Evaluations conducted by our interdisciplinary team of design au- tomation researchers and superconducting hardware experts con- firm that the resulting flow produces complete, manufacturing- ready layouts that comply with the physical design rules at the push of a button. That is, it operates fully automatically within seconds to a few minutes, and solves complex instances up to 25x faster than the state of the art. All methods are released as the fully open-source tool mqt-scpd as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit, providing the first readily usable, end- to-end design flow for planar superconducting quantum chips that explicitly addresses the underlying physical characteristics and requirements.

abstracts.value: We determine the two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private, and secret-key capacities of the pure-loss bosonic channel under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon-number constraint. For transmissivity $η$ and mean photon number $N$, all four capacities coincide and are given by $g(N)-g((1-η)N)$, where $g$ is the entropy of a thermal mode. This resolves the longstanding energy-constrained capacity problem by establishing the optimality of the reverse-coherent-information rate introduced in 2009. Our central tool is sector teleportation simulation, which we develop specifically to transfer the input-energy constraint to the shared entanglement resource, thereby preserving the constraint throughout converse arguments for general adaptive protocols. For every $N>0$, we further show that the corresponding strong-converse thresholds coincide with the unconstrained value $-\log_2(1-η)$. For parallel protocols with a hard total-photon-number cutoff, the same energy-constrained capacity formula instead satisfies an exponential strong converse. As an extension, we determine the energy-constrained two-way capacities of the quantum-limited amplifier, showing that classical assistance does not improve its unassisted quantum and private rates. Together, these results establish a unified finite-energy framework for adaptive bosonic communication and reveal how energy constraints fundamentally reshape both attainable rates and converse bounds.

titles.title: Energy-constrained two-way capacities of pure-loss and quantum-limited amplifier channels

abstracts.value: The eigenstate quantum-mechanical bootstrap can converge to the physical moment set while remaining nonexact at every finite order. We prove this for a one-dimensional quasi-exactly solvable sextic oscillator at explicitly known eigenvalues, including excited levels. At every finite order, the lower and upper bounds on $u^2$ remain strictly below and above its physical value, even after adjoining arbitrary finite polynomial Gram tests and all eigenstate-annihilator relations visible in the retained moment space. Hence neither side of the centered observable admits a finite sum-of-squares certificate modulo the eigenstate annihilator. The gap persists under any finite set of additional localizing constraints whose weights are strictly positive on polynomial vectors. We then prove convergence for polynomial Schrödinger operators satisfying explicit sum-of-squares confinement and derivative bounds. The eigenstate relations give moment estimates uniform in the truncation order; these yield a regular Schrödinger representation supported on the prescribed eigenspace. Finally, a four-mode extension combines this fixed-observable obstruction with feasible position moments having no positive representing measure at every finite order. At level three, this construction yields nonphysical feasible points with strictly positive definite moment matrices.

titles.title: Convergence Without Finite Exactness in the Eigenstate Quantum Bootstrap

abstracts.value: HOMFLY-PT polynomials describe analytic continuation of Wilson averages in Chern-Simons theory to arbitrary complex values of two independent parameters $q$ and $A$. They also depend on the knot and representation of the gauge group. However, when $q^2$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity, e.g. $q=\pm e^{iπ/m}$, these polynomials exhibit a universal (knot-independent) factorization: $H_R$ becomes the product of the polynomials for the $m$-core of the Young diagram $R$ and of one and the same factor $H_{[m]}$ for every $m$-ribbon of $R$. In all the examples which we computed this factor is just the special polynomial at $A^m$. At $q=\pm1$ factorization follows from the singularity of the cabled HOMFLY, which is the same for all representations. At $m>1$ the relevant singularity is in the projector, and what survives of it is a finite sum of braids $X_m$-- the $m$-th power sum inside the cable, which can be freely moved through the other strands. For the proof we use the Murnaghan-Nakayama rule and the Adams operation. Discovery of this hidden structure explains the old factorization puzzle.

titles.title: What a knot sees at a root of unity

abstracts.value: For perfect state transfer (PST) on unweighted mixed graphs, we classify the normalized transfer times of complete PST classes. A finite set $Λ\subset\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ containing zero occurs at a nonstationary periodic vertex if and only if $\cos(2π(x-y))\in\mathbb Q$ for all $x,y\inΛ$. Every admissible set has a connected oriented realization. We also classify the possible return phases of oriented realizations at the minimum vertex period. Transfers at rational multiples of the common minimum vertex period partition a complete class into sets of size at most six, or at most three in an oriented graph with return phase $-1$; both bounds are sharp. We construct complete classes of every finite size, including classes in which all transfers between distinct vertices occur at irrational multiples of the period and no switching automorphism maps a class vertex to a distinct class vertex. We also characterize simultaneous realization in connected oriented graphs with prescribed relative minimum vertex periods and return phases. The proof combines an imaginary quadratic field restriction with an unweighted construction that selects the complete target set.

titles.title: Perfect state transfer on mixed graphs: complete classes and transfer times

abstracts.value: Whether the spin-1/2 Aharonov-Bohm Hamiltonian supports bound states has remained controversial since Hagen concluded that no such states exist for a Dirac particle. Here, we show that Hagen's solution corresponds to a particular member of the one-parameter family of self-adjoint extensions that describe the singular Zeeman interaction, and we identify which member the microscopic physics selects. Matching the extension parameter to a finite-radius flux tube yields $ν=0$ precisely at $g=2$, and it does so in every flux sector. The critical $g$ factor is therefore universal, $g_c=2$, and depends on neither the flux sector nor the regularization radius. The flux sector controls the depth of the bound state energy, and we obtain a closed-form expression showing that binding deepens markedly with the integer part of the flux. Hagen's conclusion is thus confirmed and sharpened: it is not a statement about one arbitrary member of a family of extensions, but about the member that the physics selects when the magnetic moment takes its Dirac value, and an anomalous moment is a necessary and sufficient condition for binding in the singular channel.

titles.title: Universal critical $g$ factor for spin-1/2 Aharonov-Bohm bound states

abstracts.value: Local-basis Shannon entropies of critical wave functions contain universal subleading information, but the Shannon point of the critical transverse-field Ising chain is singular in the conventional Rényi approach. We treat it directly at $n=1$ by representing the complete computational-basis Born distribution as the odd-degree boundary of independent long-range Bernoulli edges. The Shannon chain rule separates the entropy into explicit independent-edge and conditional cycle-space terms. For the periodic chain this isolates the analytic edge anomaly and organizes the remaining constant by linked vertex support. Conditional on the stated finite-part matching and forest assumptions, every nonvanishing linked coefficient is represented by an explicit finite-dimensional integral, giving an all-orders analytic hierarchy; the four-vertex term is evaluated in closed form, and the first few linked sectors already nearly saturate the established periodic constant, which is also reconstructed independently from the exact finite-size distribution. For an interval, the exterior reduces exactly to one ghost vertex and the explicit squared logarithms cancel, leaving the analytic edge contribution $γ_E=\log2/4-1/16$. The conditional cycle term has an exact all-support decomposition into physical-line and ghost-linked sectors; conditional on closure of the boundary forest subtraction, these sectors define an all-orders hierarchy of renormalized line and monomer--dimer boundary periods for the remaining logarithmic coefficient. The first complete augmented linked coefficient is evaluated in closed form, with an exact cancellation between its line and ghost boundary-layer anomalies; an independent reconstruction from exact finite-size probabilities recovers the established coefficient $γ_1=0.060020(3)$.

titles.title: Analytical results for the Shannon entropy of the critical transverse-field Ising chain

abstracts.value: We study $SO(2n)$ gauge theories with a degenerate curvature kinetic operator defined by an orthogonal complex structure. The kinetic image is $\su(n)$, while the adjoint vacuum has stabilizer $U(n)$. We distinguish fixed projectors, unrestricted adjoint Higgs fields, and Higgs fields constrained exactly to the orbit $SO(2n)/U(n)$. For the constrained theory with a positive Higgs kinetic coefficient, the coset connection is auxiliary and the central connection is null. A nonlinear Dirac analysis establishes a regular weak-curvature branch with $2(n^2-1)$ physical degrees of freedom in four dimensions, locally equivalent to $SU(n)$ Yang--Mills theory. Normal Higgs displacements in the unrestricted theory can change the kinetic rank, so this count does not extend to that field space. We also characterize possible algebraic branches. We express the Stelle--West Higgs--gravity action through a common Clifford involution, and introduce projected Pontryagin theories and a full-rank equivariant completion.

titles.title: Projected Yang-Mills Theory and the MacDowell-Mansouri Analogy

abstracts.value: A gap between achievable rates and converse bounds persists for energy-constrained bosonic communication in the presence of excess noise. We derive a unified adaptive weak-converse bound for thermal attenuation, noisy amplification, and additive Gaussian noise under an unconditional mean transmitted-photon-number constraint. The bound applies to arbitrary adaptive protocols with quantum memories and constrains the two-way quantum, entanglement-distribution, private, and secret-key capacities. It vanishes throughout the entanglement-breaking region and approaches the corresponding PLOB bound at infinite energy. At finite energy, it improves the evaluated Gaussian squashed-entanglement and PLOB bounds in relevant parameter regimes, while comparison with hashing rates quantifies the remaining gap to achievability. The result provides a common energy-dependent benchmark for noisy bosonic Gaussian channels and extends finite-energy converse methods beyond the quantum-limited setting.

titles.title: Energy-constrained two-way capacity bounds for noisy Gaussian channels

abstracts.value: Provable guarantees for preparing quantum Gibbs states, such as rapid mixing or gapped coherent preparation paths, are known only for restricted Hamiltonian families and usually must be re-derived for each new family. Building on homomorphic polynomial transduction, a generalization of decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) and Hamiltonian DQI (HDQI), we show how relative decoding transfers such a guarantee from a source Hamiltonian $H_A$ to a target $H_B$. Writing each Hamiltonian as a sum of $m$ Pauli terms, the subsets of terms whose product is proportional to the identity, its relations, form a binary linear code, $K_A$ for the source and $K_B$ for the target, with the Pauli-label matrix as parity-check matrix as in DQI. Starting from the canonical thermofield double (TFD) of $H_A$, a Bell transform, a reversible label map, and a coherent decoder for the quotient code $K_B/K_A$ prepare an approximate TFD of $H_B$, and hence its Gibbs state. Because this decoder only resolves target relations absent from the source, the reachable inverse temperature is set by the relative distance $d_{\rm rel}$, the fewest terms in any such relation. It can far exceed the ordinary distance $d_{\rm ord}$, the fewest terms in any target relation, which bounds the uniform exact decoding radius of DQI and HDQI. We show that linear $d_{\rm rel}$ with efficient decoding at linear radius certifies a constant inverse temperature. As an example, starting from a nearest-neighbor spin chain whose TFD is known to be preparable at every finite temperature, a sparse classical parity-check matrix yields bounded-degree, geometrically nonlocal, noncommuting targets with $d_{\rm ord}=3$ and $d_{\rm rel}=Θ(m)$. To our knowledge, this gives a new class of efficiently preparable TFDs.

titles.title: Quantum Gibbs State Preparation via Relative Decoding: From Fast-Mixing Sources to Broader Target Classes
